name: Claude Code, on your own machine
operator: Anthropic (the vendor); each user is the operator of their own deployment
basis: the vendor’s own documentation and a published deployment shape
what: The command-line coding agent, running as the user’s own account on their machine, with the settings it ships with.
note: An example scan of a product as its vendor documents it, not of any one deployment. Disclosure: the agent that wrote this scan runs on this product.

grant.product: Claude Code (the CLI, on your own machine)
grant.statement: This describes a published deployment shape. It is not an assessment, an audit, a certification or a security review of any named product, and it carries no adjective and no score.

I04.n: The vendor calls it "an agentic coding tool that reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands".

I08.n: It edits files, runs commands, stages changes, commits and opens pull requests.

I10.n: The codebase, the shell, git and the development tools it integrates with.

I11.n: It can connect to Model Context Protocol servers; a project’s servers have their own approval prompt.

I12.n: Agent teams coordinate several instances, each in its own context, that message each other. The vendor says they "are experimental and disabled by default".

I16.n: In Manual mode, which the person chooses, shell commands and edits ask before they run; file reads in the working directory do not.

I18.n: From v2.1.283, auto mode is the built-in starting mode for terminal and VS Code sessions: a classifier reviews actions instead of prompting; an action it blocks is listed, and the person can approve it so Claude may retry.
I18.span: approve the action so Claude may retry

I20.n: The vendor states what the product is for.

I21.n: Allow, ask and deny rules per tool and pattern.

I22.n: The security page states limits, for example that an approved shell command can write anywhere the account can.

I23.n: A published deployment shape lists 16 capabilities from 22 tool rows; it says none of the rows is measured and all 22 are derived.

I38.n: In Manual mode, which the person chooses, shell commands beyond a read-only set and edits need approval.

I39.n: Esc stops the current response or tool call mid-turn, and Ctrl+C interrupts a running operation.
I39.span: Stop the current response or tool call mid-turn so you can redirect

I41.n: Tool activity can be exported as OpenTelemetry events; it is configured by the operator.

I43.n: Usage, cost and tool activity across an organisation, through OpenTelemetry.

I45.n: Sandboxing restricts shell commands at the operating system level (filesystem and network) on macOS, Linux and WSL2; on native Windows, commands run unsandboxed. The page says it is off by default, that it covers shell commands only while the file tools, MCP servers and hooks run outside it, and that Claude can ask to run a command unsandboxed unless strict sandbox mode is on.
I45.span: The sandbox is off by default

I46.n: "The boundary is a permission prompt, so a Bash command you approve can still write anywhere your user account can."
I46.span: a Bash command you approve can still write anywhere your user account can

I48.n: An organisation can deliver managed settings, and nothing in a user's own settings files or the --settings flag overrides a managed key. This is an enforcement mechanism, not a policy. It applies only where an organisation deploys managed settings.

I56.n: By default its commits carry a Co-Authored-By trailer naming the Claude model in use; a setting can change or hide it.

I57.n: A feedback command and a bug command send reports to the vendor.

I58.n: A page describes what data is sent, kept and used.

I61.n: The model configuration page lists the models it uses by alias (Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, Fable) and the version each alias resolves to for each provider.
I61.span: Uses the latest Opus model for complex reasoning tasks

I63.n: The vendor points to a SOC 2 Type 2 report and an ISO 27001 certificate at its trust centre; they cover the vendor, not a user’s deployment.

S2.n: The vendor’s community marketplace holds third-party plugins their authors submitted, and the page says many plugins sit in their authors’ own marketplaces.
S2.span: Third-party plugins that their authors submitted to Anthropic

S3.n: The documentation publishes an llms.txt index.

configurations.name: As shipped
configurations.note: Auto mode, the built-in starting mode for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions from v2.1.283 (on earlier versions only on Pro, Max, Ultra and Team plans): a classifier reviews actions instead of the person. claude -p and the Agent SDK start in Manual mode; auto mode needs a supported model, and an organisation can turn it off.

configurations.name: Sandbox on
configurations.note: Shell commands confined by the operating system.

configurations.name: Manual mode
configurations.note: The person chooses Manual mode: shell commands and edits ask first.

configurations.name: Managed by an organisation
configurations.note: Managed settings, permission rules and telemetry.

configurations.name: With tools and agent teams
configurations.note: Everything that widens what it does.

moved: As above. Managed settings are recorded as an enforcement mechanism, not as a policy in force.

findings.finding: The quoted span "Stripe rolled out Claude Code to 1,370 engineers." is not in the source. The page (read 2026-11-10) says "Deployed Claude Code to 1,370 engineers with a zero-configuration setup". The fact and the figure are right; the span is a paraphrase presented as a quotation. Quote the page exactly, under fifteen words, or drop the span.

"The product and its model family are named" is not what the indicator asks (the models and third-party components it uses are listed). I searched the overview page and found no model named. Either cite a page that lists the models (the model configuration page), or remove the answer.

The note says most rows are "derived, not measured". The profile itself says all 22 of its rows are derived and none measured ("every row is a claim until somebody runs the probes"). Say none are measured. Grade documented is right for the profile as a document; the scope for I23 says a grant profile only, which the source is.

The source cited (permissions) supports "a deny rule removes a tool" and the person can decline a prompt. Neither is a way to pause or stop the agent. I did not find an interrupt or stop statement on that page. Cite a page that says the person can interrupt a running session, or lower the credit.

Credited as available (auto mode). The source says in auto mode "a classifier reviews actions instead of you". The indicator is that the person approves critical decisions only; a classifier standing in for the person is a different fact. Round two will argue whether this credit holds.

The page tells an author how to publish a marketplace and says "anyone with access registers it". That shows the mechanism, not that any third party has published one. The scope asks for third parties publishing. Cite a page that names third-party plugins or marketplaces, or lower the credit.

The span "Claude Code is an AI-powered coding assistant" is in the source and under fifteen words. But it is the documentation describing the product to a reader, not the agent telling the people it talks to that it is an AI. Weak credit for this indicator; consider whether it should stand.

Grade documented, mode available, source the sandbox page. The scope says this indicator is read from a measured grant only, and the grant is derived. The answer is accurate; the credit should come from the grant, not from the page. Check how the scorer treats it.

Opened each source. The note says what the source says; grade documented is right for each (S3 observed: llms.txt fetched, resolves); mode is right (I11, I12, I18, I21, I41, I43, I45, I48 are available and tied to a configuration; the rest are the default). Spans in I46 (13 words) and I56 (7) are in the source. Quoted text in I04 (12 words) and I12 is in the source. I63 credit is limited, as the note says, to the vendor.
The "max" configuration is "Auto mode, tools and agent teams": the three flags it turns on exist (auto, mcp, teams) and each is documented. No finding.

The scan contradicts itself, and the page it now cites says why. The permission modes page (read 2026-11-10): "With Claude Code v2.1.283 or later, auto mode is the built-in starting permission mode for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions. On earlier versions, it is the built-in starting permission mode only on Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans." The scan marks I18 available (auto), keeps I16 and I38 as default on "Manual mode", and its "As shipped" configuration says "Manual mode: shell commands and edits ask first". The studio saw this in its own I18 response and left it. If auto is the starting mode, then as shipped on a current version the classifier reviews actions instead of the person, I18 is default, and the Manual-mode answers describe a mode a person chooses. Decide which version the scan describes, say so in the configuration notes, and set the modes to match. This changes what the card means for A, so it blocks sign-off.

Argued against Autonomy 3, which rests on S1 and I18. The span is exact (10 words) and the fact is a named customer with a figure. But the figure is a rollout count: "Deployed Claude Code to 1,370 engineers". The scope asks for usage figures for the capability that acts, and a count of engineers who have it installed does not say that the agent completed anything. The same page lists, among Stripe's own results, an education program "that reframed AI assistants as capable new engineers who need context, not replacements who work autonomously". A3 is "completes routine tasks end to end in production; a person handles exceptions". The page the card cites for it says the customer does not treat it as working autonomously. The Scala to Java migration on the page ("10,000 lines in four days") is one task, with AI assistance. S1 stands only on the literal test. Two options: find a usage figure for what the agent did (sessions, pull requests, tasks), or state on the card that S1 is a rollout count. The Manus card has the stronger kind of figure (sessions).

Argued against Control 4. Under the Spectrum reading (data/indicators.json) a documented limit enforced outside the agent counts, and the note says the operator turns the sandbox on. The note leaves out what the sandboxing page says in three places: "The sandbox is off by default"; it "wraps shell commands" and the built-in file tools "run outside it"; and "Claude can ask to run a command unsandboxed" (excludedCommands and unsandboxed retries, with strict sandbox mode to turn the retry off). So C4 rests on a boundary that is opt in, covers shell commands only, and has a documented way for the agent to ask out of it. Add those three facts to the note so the card does not read as a boundary around the whole agent. A better statement of enforcement outside the model is on the permissions page: "Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model."

The second fact of Control 4, available (managed). The settings page does say managed settings sit above user, project and local files. As the note says, it is a mechanism. It applies only where an organisation deploys it. Control 4 therefore needs two opt-in facts, sandbox and managed settings. Say so on the card; with no managed settings and no sandbox the card is Control 2 at most on the default.

Control 3 (I41, I39, I43). I39 is default and its source is right: "Stop the current response or tool call mid-turn so you can redirect" (12 words, exact, interactive mode page). I41 and I43 are available (managed), exported OpenTelemetry events. I43 says it is monitored in operation; the page documents the export and the metrics, not that anybody looks. Acceptable on the Spectrum reading of available. Same condition as I48.

Re-sourced to the settings reference. True: "Default: unset, so Claude Code adds Co-Authored-By: <name> and the vendor's no-reply address. The name is the model in use when the commit is made, such as Claude Sonnet 5." and "attribution.commit Change or hide the trailer". The span is the second sentence of that, which does not by itself say it is an AI; the trailer sentence does. Use "Claude Code adds Co-Authored-By: <name> and the vendor's no-reply address" or similar (under 15 words). The note says pull request descriptions get "a Generated with Claude Code line"; the page says "pull request descriptions get plain text" and gives no wording. Remove the wording or cite where it is written. The mode is right as default, and the note already says a setting can hide it.

The span "Third-party plugins that their authors submitted to Anthropic" (8 words) is exact on the Anthropic marketplaces page. It names a marketplace that holds third-party plugins. It is the vendor describing them; that is what the indicator asks. Round one finding answered.

Model configuration page lists the aliases (Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, Fable) and what each resolves to. The span "Uses the latest Opus model for complex reasoning tasks" (9 words) is exact. Round one finding answered.
The note now says 16 capabilities from 22 tool rows, none measured, all derived. That is what the profile says. Round one finding answered. On a card the Spectrum reading counts it.
The S1 span is now the page's words. I39 is re-sourced to the interactive mode page and the span is exact. Both round one findings answered.

Levels three and four on the card: A4, C4. A4: A3 (I08, I18, S1) with I10 default and I18. The argument is above: the mode of I18 may make it default, which strengthens the chain, while S1 is a rollout count that the customer itself says is not autonomous work. C4: two opt-in facts, with caveats above. R2 (I10, I11), O2 (I22, I58, I61) not argued; they are not level three or four. Verdict changes: the contradiction in the modes must be settled before a level is read off this card.

Round two asked for three facts in the note; the note now has them and each is true on the sandboxing page (read 2026-11-10): "The sandbox is off by default", the sandbox covers shell commands only while file tools run outside it, and "Claude can ask to run a command unsandboxed" with allowUnsandboxedCommands false as the way to turn that off. But the page the answer cites, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing, is not in the scan's captures, so it has no recorded hash, and Control 4 rests on it. Run tools/capture.mjs for this scan so the page is captured and hashed. The same page also says commands run unsandboxed on native Windows and that MCP servers and hooks run outside the sandbox; the note could carry the Windows line, since the card is read as a boundary for the terminal product. Partly answered.

The caveat finding is answered: the note now says it applies only where an organisation deploys managed settings, and the settings page does say "Nothing in your own settings files or --settings overrides a managed key". Two problems remain in the note. First, "hooks run on every tool call and can block it" is not on the cited settings page (it shows a hooks example and says no hooks run by default; I found no statement there that hooks block a call), and the hooks page is not a source of the scan. Cite a captured page that says it, or cut the clause. Second, a full stop is missing: "not a policy It applies only where" should read "not a policy. It applies only where". Partly answered.

Round two must-fix answered. Verified on the permission modes page: "With Claude Code v2.1.283 or later, auto mode is the built-in starting permission mode for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions"; the span "approve the action so Claude may retry" is exact (7 words) and the blocked-action text matches. I18 is default, I16 and I38 are available under the new Manual mode configuration, "As shipped" says auto mode, and no answer still describes Manual mode as the start. Left out of the notes, from the same page: below v2.1.283 the start is auto only on Pro, Max, Ultra and Team plans (v2.1.228 or later is needed for the built-in auto default at all); claude -p and the Agent SDK start in Manual; auto mode requires a supported model and an organisation can turn it off. A reader on an older version or a managed machine gets a different As shipped. One clause in the configuration note would cover it. The indicator is a person approving critical decisions only; here a classifier decides first and the person approves what it blocks, which the studio argued in round one and I leave as a judgement for sign-off.

Answered. The span "so Claude Code adds Co-Authored-By: <name>" is exact on the settings reference (7 words), the note says what the page says (trailer naming the model in use; attribution.commit changes or hides it), and the pull request wording is gone. The credit stays weak for the indicator: the trailer is read by people reviewing commits, not by people the agent talks to. Openness 1 does not depend on it, since I22 gives the same level.

Changed-answer check of mode and grade: documented and available with cfg sandbox is right for an opt-in sandbox; the indicator scope allows a documented sandbox on a Spectrum card if the note says what enforces it, and the note does.

Card A4 R2 C4 O2 (computed). A4 is I08 and I18 for Acts, then I10 default for the second step; I12 (agent teams, experimental and disabled by default) is an alternative. Without I18 the card falls to A2 on I16 (Manual, available), so Autonomy rests on one fact whose truth depends on version, plan and organisation policy; without I10 it stays A4 through I12. C4 is I45 plus I48, both opt in, and the notes now say so (shell commands only, escape hatch, managed settings only where deployed); remove either and Control is 3, held by I41, I39, I43, of which I41 and I43 are available under managed settings. Control 4 is therefore not a property of the product as shipped; the card must show its configuration. S1 is gone and Autonomy does not use it. The publication rule (level one or more in at least one dimension) is met many times over.
